posts.searchText: Best way to push contacts into Salesforce We get CSV exports today. Anyone using a cleaner Salesforce import mapping for title, company, and LinkedIn URL fields? Map Email as external ID when possible, keep Company as Account Name match, and store LinkedIn URL in a custom field. Deduplicate before import. posts.title: Database Providers vs Apollo.io: Which Fits Your Use Case? | Community | Database Providers
posts.metaDescription: A one-time compiled file versus a credit-metered platform. What each model costs you, and which one fits how your team actually works.
posts.searchText: Database Providers vs Apollo.io: Which Fits Your Use Case? | Community | Database Providers My team is comparing Apollo against buying a list outright. We are a small sales team, mostly running one or two campaigns a quarter. Which way should we go? The choice is not really about data quality — it is about whether your team uses contact data daily or occasionally, because the two models price for completely different usage patterns. Apollo is a sales engagement platform with a database attached. Access is metered by credits and seats, and the value comes from SDRs living in the tool — prospecting, enriching, sequencing and dialling inside one workflow. If your reps are in a contact database every day, that integration is worth paying for, and a one-time file will feel clumsy by comparison. On the pattern you describe, that is the case where Apollo genuinely wins. Where it stops fitting is exactly your situation. One or two campaigns a quarter means you are paying a seat and credit structure across the months where nobody opens the tool. Credits expire on their schedule, not yours. And when the subscription ends, continued access to the data ends with it — what you keep is what you exported while you were paying. Database Providers works the other way. You specify a segment, we compile and verify the file at order time, and you own it outright. No seat licence, no credit balance, no renewal date, and the file does not stop working when you stop paying. For a team running campaigns in bursts, that maps to how the spend actually occurs. The honest trade-off: you do not get a sequencing tool, a dialler, or live enrichment inside your CRM. You get a dataset, delivered as CSV or Excel with headers matched to your destination system. If you need the workflow layer, you need a platform — and you should buy one rather than trying to make a file do that job. The other difference worth checking before you decide is coverage in your specific segment. Platform databases are broad but uneven, and depth varies sharply by vertical and geography. Ask both of us for a count and a sample on your exact target segment, run them through your own verification tool, and compare the results rather than the marketing claims. That comparison answers the question better than any feature table. Apollo's pricing, credit policy and contract terms are published on their own site and change over time — check them directly rather than relying on a third-party summary, including ours. Compliance note for healthcare outreach in the US: CAN-SPAM governs the send, but if your messaging touches patient data or clinical claims, FDA promotional rules and your own regulatory review apply on top. Physician contact data is business contact information and is not protected health information, so HIPAA does not apply to the list itself — but it does apply to anything a recipient sends back to you.

posts.title: GDPR-friendly outreach with purchased B2B lists
posts.metaDescription: Using purchased B2B data in Europe requires careful sourcing, lawful-basis assessment, transparency, suppression handling and outreach rules that fit each market.
posts.searchText: GDPR-friendly outreach with purchased B2B lists Can we use a purchased B2B contact list for outreach in Europe without creating GDPR problems? Purchased B2B data is not automatically GDPR-compliant simply because it contains work contact details. Before outreach, document where the data came from, what fields were collected, the intended use, your lawful-basis assessment, and how people will be informed about the processing. You should also maintain opt-out and suppression controls and check the electronic-marketing rules that apply in each target country. Your legal or privacy team should approve the final outreach process for your specific use case. The biggest issue for us was not the list purchase itself but proving the source and setting up a clear process for notices, objections and suppression. We also separated countries instead of treating all European outreach the same, because email and direct-marketing requirements can differ by market. Ask the provider for sourcing and compliance documentation before importing anything into your CRM.

posts.title: How Many Cardiologists Can I Reach in Texas? | Community | Database Providers
posts.metaDescription: Reachable cardiologist records in Texas, why the number is lower than the licensed population, and how to segment what remains.
posts.searchText: How Many Cardiologists Can I Reach in Texas? | Community | Database Providers We sell a cardiac imaging product and want to run a Texas-only campaign. Before I ask for a quote, roughly how many cardiologists are actually reachable by email there? I need to know if the segment is big enough to justify a campaign at all. Our verified cardiologist coverage runs to roughly 8,200 records across the United States, and Texas is one of the three deepest states in that set — enough volume to run a readable state-only campaign, though not enough to run several in parallel. Ask for the exact Texas count before you build the plan, because it moves as the file is recompiled. The gap between that number and the licensed cardiologist population in Texas is worth understanding, because it changes how you segment. A large share of cardiologists work inside hospital systems where the practice email is gatekept and never appears in any commercial dataset. Many practise under a group entity rather than their own name. Some hold multiple affiliations, which produces duplicates that have to be resolved down to one record. What remains after all of that is the reachable set — and it is always smaller than the licence roll. For a cardiac imaging product specifically, the practical move is to segment on practice affiliation rather than title alone. A cardiologist in an independent or small-group practice has meaningfully more purchasing influence over imaging equipment than one inside a large hospital system, where the decision sits with a procurement committee and a radiology director. Filtering on that split typically produces a smaller list that performs better, and it usually means adding hospital administrators and radiology leads as a second segment rather than trying to reach the physician directly. Tell us the practice-size band and whether you want the hospital-side contacts included, and we will return the exact Texas count plus a free sample drawn from that segment so you can run it through your own verification before committing. Healthcare outreach in the US: CAN-SPAM governs the send, but if your messaging touches patient data or clinical claims, FDA promotional rules and your own regulatory review apply on top. Physician contact data is business contact information and is not protected health information, so HIPAA does not apply to the list itself — but it does apply to anything a recipient sends back to you.

posts.title: Is It Legal to Buy an Email List in Germany? | Community | Database Providers
posts.metaDescription: Germany is the strictest major B2B email market. What UWG requires before you send, and how to build a list that works within it.
posts.searchText: Is It Legal to Buy an Email List in Germany? | Community | Database Providers We are expanding into the DACH region and want to run outbound to German manufacturing firms. Someone on our legal team said buying a list is illegal in Germany. Is that actually true, or are they being overly cautious? Buying the data is not illegal in Germany — sending to it without consent generally is, and that distinction is what your legal team is reacting to. German courts have consistently read the UWG as requiring prior consent for commercial email, including business-to-business, which makes Germany the strictest of the major European markets. There is no broad B2B carve-out of the kind the UK gives corporate subscribers or the Netherlands allows under legitimate interest. What this means practically for a DACH expansion: Email-first outbound into Germany does not work the way it does in the US or UK. Teams that succeed there use the purchased data differently — as an account and contact map for LinkedIn outreach, telephone contact within the permitted rules, event invitations, and targeted advertising audiences. The data is the targeting layer, not the send list. If email is essential, consent has to be collected first. That means a German-language landing page, a gated asset worth downloading, and an opt-in that meets UWG standards — with the purchased file used to drive traffic to it through paid channels rather than through the inbox. This is why we ask which market you are targeting before we build a file. For Germany we will tell you plainly that a standard outbound list is the wrong instrument, and we will build the account-mapping file instead — firmographics, decision-maker names and titles, and company-level detail, without positioning it as something you can cold-email. Our German coverage sits in the manufacturing and industrial verticals where it is deepest, and we will show you the count for your exact segment before you commit to anything. This is general guidance, not legal advice. Your obligations depend on your entity, your channel mix and your use of the data — confirm with German counsel before launch. Adding the operational side: Austria follows Germany closely, so treat DACH as one regime rather than three. Switzerland is the exception — it operates an opt-out model for B2B, which makes it the practical entry point for a DACH campaign. Several clients start in Switzerland to prove the offer, then move into Germany through consented channels once they have case studies in the local language.

posts.title: My Bounce Rate Spiked and I Don't Know Why | Community | Database Providers
posts.metaDescription: A bounce spike after a purchased-list send usually traces to file age, not record quality. How to diagnose it in the right order.
posts.searchText: My Bounce Rate Spiked and I Don't Know Why | Community | Database Providers First send on a new list and my bounce rate came back at 14%. The sample I tested a few weeks ago was clean. My ESP is threatening to suspend the account. I don't know whether to blame the file or something I did. A bounce spike on a first send almost always traces to file age rather than record quality — and the detail in your message points straight at it. You tested the sample a few weeks ago, which means the file has been sitting while people changed roles, companies restructured and mailboxes were retired. B2B contact data degrades continuously from the day it is compiled, so a gap between verification and send is the single most common cause of exactly this number. Work through it in this order before concluding anything: Check the compile date on the file, not the purchase date. If more than two weeks separate compilation from your send, re-verify before doing anything else. Check whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC are aligned on the sending domain. An authentication failure produces rejections that many platforms report in the same bucket as hard bounces. Check how your ESP classifies deferrals. Some platforms count soft bounces and deferrals into the headline figure, which can turn a healthy 4% into an alarming 14% without a single bad record. Check whether old CRM contacts were merged into the same campaign. Stale in-house data mixed with a fresh file is a frequent culprit, and the blame lands on the purchased list by default. On your immediate problem: stop sending, pull the bounce log, and separate hard from soft before you talk to your ESP. Going back to them with a classified breakdown is what gets an account reinstated. This is the reason we compile and verify at order time rather than pulling from a stored archive — your file is dated to your purchase, not to whenever the underlying database was last touched. If your hard bounce rate is meaningfully above what the sample showed, send us the log with your order ID and we will review the affected records and replace them from the same segment. That process is straightforward in the first weeks after delivery and much harder once a file has aged past a full quarter, so raise it now rather than after the next send. One compliance note for healthcare outreach in the US: CAN-SPAM governs the send, but if your messaging touches patient data or clinical claims, FDA promotional rules and your own regulatory review apply on top. Physician contact data is business contact information and is not protected health information, so HIPAA does not apply to the list itself — but it does apply to anything a recipient sends back to you.

posts.title: Which Email List Should a SaaS Company Buy to Reach HR Managers? | Community | Database Providers
posts.metaDescription: How to specify an HR contact list for SaaS outbound — which filters change the message, which waste volume, and what to buy first.
posts.searchText: Which Email List Should a SaaS Company Buy to Reach HR Managers? | Community | Database Providers We are a 45-person HR tech SaaS company. First time buying data. I have budget for one list and I don't want to get this wrong. What should I actually be asking for? For a first HR-tech purchase, specify on two axes and stay loose on everything else: HR function at decision-making seniority, and the company-size band where your product actually works. Those two determine whether the message makes sense to the reader and whether the deal is possible at all. Every additional filter multiplies the reduction in available records, and a list narrowed on five axes is usually too small to learn anything from. The specification that matters, in order: Function over title string. Targeting 'HR Manager' as a keyword misses Head of People, People Operations Lead, Talent Director and a dozen other variants of the same buyer. Ask for the HR function with a seniority band, not a title match. Company size as a hard filter. Most HR tech has a real floor and ceiling — a tool built for 200-person companies fails at 20 and fails at 20,000. Set that boundary firmly, because contacts outside it waste send volume and generate the complaints that damage sender reputation. Industry only if your pitch changes. If you would send the identical email to a logistics firm and a law firm, industry segmentation costs you records and buys you nothing. Our global HR coverage runs to roughly 653K records, with about 415K in the United States — deep enough that you can afford to be specific on function and seniority without dropping below a workable volume. On sizing: work backwards from pipeline. If you need ten opportunities and roughly a third of meetings convert, that is around thirty meetings, which at a 2% positive reply rate means a list in the low thousands. Buy to what you can actually send over the next six to eight weeks, not more — data decays from the day it is compiled, and the tail of an oversized file will be stale before you reach it. One structural point that matters for a 45-person company testing a channel: this is a one-time purchase. No seat licence, no credit balance to burn down, no annual renewal. You own the file. That is the difference between testing outbound as a channel and committing to a platform contract before you know whether it works. Send us the function, seniority band and company-size range and we will return a free sample from that exact segment. Run it through your own verification tool before you buy the full volume — that is what the sample is for. Note for healthcare outreach in the US: CAN-SPAM governs the send, but if your messaging touches patient data or clinical claims, FDA promotional rules and your own regulatory review apply on top. Physician contact data is business contact information and is not protected health information, so HIPAA does not apply to the list itself — but it does apply to anything a recipient sends back to you.

guides.searchText: Choosing the right B2B segment How to pick industry, title, and geography filters so your list matches campaign goals. A good segment is narrow enough to personalize, wide enough to fill pipeline. Start from the offer - Who can buy or influence this product? - Which titles actually reply in your past campaigns? - Which geos can you support with follow-up? Common mistakes - Mixing too many industries in one send. - Targeting C-level only when managers own the workflow. - Ignoring company size when your pricing is SMB-only. Talk with your account team about what has worked for your niche.

guides.title: How to improve email list deliverability
guides.summary: Practical checklist for verification, suppression, and sending practices that keep bounce rates low.
guides.searchText: How to improve email list deliverability Practical checklist for verification, suppression, and sending practices that keep bounce rates low. Deliverability problems usually come from stale contacts, weak targeting, or aggressive sending — not from one bad export. Before you send - Suppress known unsubscribes and hard bounces. - Prefer recently verified segments for cold outreach. - Align titles and industries with your ICP before volume ramps. Sending hygiene - Warm domains gradually; avoid blasting a brand-new domain. - Keep subject lines and body copy relevant to the persona. - Monitor bounce and complaint rates after each batch. When bounce is high Share sample bounce codes (without contact PII) with support so we can help diagnose.
